title: Pressure-cooker beef stock
subtitle: Deep, dark stock in 90 minutes instead of six hours
excerpt: A rich beef stock made from oxtail, vegetables, and aromatics, pressure-cooked to extract maximum flavour in a fraction of the usual time. Makes about 1.5 litres.
sourceNotes: Beef stock from roasted bones is a foundation of French classical cookery, described in Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire (1903) and in the British tradition through Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861). The pressure-cooker method condenses the extraction phase from 6, 8 hours to 90 minutes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in 500 ml portions for up to 6 months. Label with the date. Defrost overnight in the fridge or from frozen in a saucepan over low heat.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a double batch when oxtail is on offer. Freeze in ice-cube trays first for small portions, then transfer to bags.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Stock keeps refrigerated for up to 5 days. The fat sets on top as it chills, lift it off before use or leave it as a seal.

content.text: Beef stock is the dark, savoury base that gives gravies, braises, and French onion soup their depth. Made from oxtail with a standard mirepoix, it comes out of the pressure cooker rich and gelatinous after 90 minutes, a job that would take the better part of a day on the hob.

The oxtail gives both body and flavour. Its high collagen content dissolves under pressure into gelatin, which is what makes a good stock set to a jelly when cold. If you roast the oxtail pieces in a hot oven for 20 minutes first, the colour deepens considerably; it is worth doing.
Strain through a fine sieve and refrigerate. The fat solidifies on top overnight and lifts off cleanly, leaving a clear, cold stock underneath. Freeze what you will not use within 5 days.
Heat the oven to 220°C. Spread the oxtail pieces in a roasting tin and roast for 20 minutes until well browned. This step is optional but adds significant colour and flavour to the finished stock.

Put the oxtail into the pressure cooker with the halved onion, carrot pieces, celery, tomato puree, bay leaves, thyme sprigs, and peppercorns. Add enough cold water to cover by 3 cm, about 1.8 litres. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 90 minutes.

Allow the pressure to release naturally for 20 minutes, then release any remaining pressure. Strain through a fine sieve into a large bowl or saucepan. Discard the solids. Cool the stock quickly, set the bowl in a sink of cold water and stir. Refrigerate overnight.

The next day, the fat will have solidified into a pale layer on the surface. Lift it off and discard. The stock beneath should be a dark amber and will have set to a light jelly: that is the gelatin from the oxtail. Reheat gently before using.

rows.symptom: The stock is thin and watery
rows.cause: Too much water was added, or the cooking time was not long enough to extract the collagen from the oxtail.
rows.fix: After straining, simmer the stock in an open saucepan over medium heat until reduced by a third. This concentrates the flavour and gelatin.

rows.cause: A rapid pressure release or vigorous boiling during cooking disturbs the proteins and fat, making the stock cloudy.
rows.fix: Cloudy stock tastes the same as clear. For a cleaner result next time, allow a full natural pressure release and avoid hard boiling during the cooking phase.

rows.symptom: The stock did not set to a jelly when cold
rows.cause: Insufficient collagen from the oxtail, or the pieces were too lean.
rows.fix: The stock is still usable, it simply has less body. Next time, source oxtail with more joint material attached, or add a split pig's trotter to the pot.

rows.cause: The oxtail was not roasted, or there was not enough tomato puree to add colour and acidity.
rows.fix: Roasting the bones first makes a significant difference. You can also reduce the finished stock by a quarter to concentrate the flavour.

content.text: Pour the cold stock into 500 ml portions in freezer-safe containers or zip-lock bags. Freeze flat for up to 6 months. Alternatively, freeze in an ice-cube tray first, then transfer to bags: each cube is roughly 30 ml, useful for deglazing pans or enriching sauces one cube at a time.

Homemade beef stock has a different character from anything that comes in a carton. It sets to a jelly in the fridge and coats the back of a spoon in a way that shop-bought stock does not. The pressure cooker puts this within reach of a weekday morning. Set it up, go about other things, strain and refrigerate. It earns its place in any freezer that sees regular braising.
